subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Minimalism in the 1960s is characterised by:
options: Simple geometric forms, repetition and industrial materials
questions.explain: Minimalism stripped art to essential geometric forms, often using repetition and impersonal industrial fabrication.

questions.q: Which colour model is used for full-colour commercial process printing?
questions.explain: Process printing uses CMYK (cyan, magenta, yellow and key/black) inks combined to reproduce a wide colour range.

questions.q: In the critical study of art, 'iconography' is the study of:
options: The price history of the work
The subject matter, symbols and their meanings within an image
questions.explain: Iconography interprets the symbols, motifs and subject matter and the meanings they carry.

questions.q: Lithography is a planographic process that relies on which fundamental principle?
options: Ink held in deeply bitten grooves
Oil and water repelling one another
Pressure forcing ink through a stencil
questions.explain: Lithography exploits the mutual repulsion of grease and water so the greasy drawn image accepts ink while the dampened blank areas reject it.

questions.q: Installation art is best defined as:
options: A three-dimensional work designed to transform the perception of a whole space
questions.explain: Installation art is created for and often fills a specific space, immersing the viewer rather than presenting a discrete object.

questions.q: A fast shutter speed (e.g. 1/1000s) is primarily used to:
questions.explain: A fast shutter speed exposes the sensor briefly and freezes rapid movement without motion blur.

questions.q: Caravaggio is a leading figure of which movement, noted for dramatic lighting?
questions.explain: Caravaggio was a Baroque master whose tenebrism used violent contrasts of light and dark for dramatic effect.

questions.q: Which textile technique is a method of surface decoration rather than construction?
questions.explain: Screen-printing decorates the surface of an existing cloth, whereas weaving, knitting and crochet construct the fabric itself.

questions.q: The personal study / contextual investigation at A-level requires students to:
options: Relate practical work to a written investigation drawing on the work of others
questions.explain: The personal investigation links practical exploration to a written/contextual study informed by the work of other artists and contexts.

questions.q: In painting, 'impasto' describes:
options: Thickly applied paint that stands proud of the surface
questions.explain: Impasto is paint laid on so thickly that it retains the marks of the brush or knife and catches the light.

questions.q: Marcel Duchamp's 'Fountain', a urinal presented as art, is an example of a:
questions.explain: Duchamp's readymades were ordinary manufactured objects designated as art, challenging notions of authorship and aesthetics.

questions.q: In a formal analysis of an artwork, you would primarily discuss:
options: Line, shape, colour, tone, texture, form and composition
questions.explain: Formal analysis examines the visual elements and how they are organised, independent of subject or context.

questions.q: In additive colour mixing (as used on screens), the primary colours are:
questions.explain: Additive (light-based) mixing uses red, green and blue, which combine to make white.

questions.q: In typography, the small finishing strokes at the ends of letters are called:
questions.explain: Serifs are the small terminal strokes; typefaces without them are described as sans-serif.

questions.q: Which artist is most strongly associated with Post-Impressionism and thickly applied, expressive brushwork in works like 'The Starry Night'?
questions.explain: Vincent van Gogh, a Post-Impressionist, is renowned for emotionally charged colour and swirling impasto brushwork.

questions.q: In the A-level investigative process, 'refining' work refers to:
options: Starting an entirely new unrelated project
Developing and improving ideas through experimentation and review
questions.explain: Refining is the ongoing development, reviewing and improving of ideas and techniques towards a resolved outcome.

questions.q: In a woven textile, the threads running lengthwise on the loom are the:
questions.explain: The warp threads are held under tension lengthwise on the loom; the weft is woven across them.

questions.q: The photographic 'rule of thirds' is a guide to:
options: Composition and placement of key elements
questions.explain: The rule of thirds divides the frame into a 3x3 grid, suggesting subjects be placed along the lines or intersections for a balanced composition.

questions.q: Which movement celebrated speed, technology, machinery and the dynamism of the modern city?
questions.explain: Italian Futurism, founded by Marinetti, glorified speed, the machine and modern urban energy.

questions.q: The term 'avant-garde' is used in art history to describe:
options: Experimental, innovative work ahead of its time
questions.explain: Avant-garde describes pioneering, experimental art that pushes beyond accepted conventions.

questions.q: Abstract Expressionism's 'action painting', exemplified by Jackson Pollock, emphasised:
options: The gestural, physical act of applying paint
questions.explain: Action painting foregrounded spontaneous, energetic gesture, as in Pollock's poured and dripped canvases.

questions.q: 'Chiaroscuro' refers to:
options: The strong contrast of light and shade to model form
The use of bold flat colour
questions.explain: Chiaroscuro is the treatment of light and dark to create the illusion of three-dimensional volume.

questions.q: Colours that sit next to each other on the colour wheel, such as blue, blue-green and green, are described as:
questions.explain: Analogous colours are neighbours on the wheel and produce harmonious, low-contrast schemes.

questions.q: The formal element that describes the perceived surface quality of a work — whether real or implied — is:
questions.explain: Texture is the actual or visual surface quality, such as roughness or smoothness, of an artwork.

questions.q: In colour theory, adding white to a hue produces a:
questions.explain: A tint is a hue lightened with white; adding black makes a shade and adding grey makes a tone.

questions.q: In typography, the vertical space between lines of text is known as:
questions.explain: Leading (from the strips of lead once used) is the distance between baselines of consecutive lines of type.

questions.q: The Renaissance development of linear perspective allowed artists to:
options: Create a convincing illusion of three-dimensional space on a flat surface
questions.explain: Linear perspective, codified by Brunelleschi and Alberti, used converging lines to a vanishing point to suggest depth.

questions.q: Fauvism is characterised above all by:
questions.explain: The Fauves, led by Matisse, used vivid, arbitrary colour for expressive rather than descriptive effect.

questions.q: On a colour wheel, colours directly opposite one another are called:
questions.explain: Complementary colours sit opposite each other and create strong contrast and vibrancy when paired.

questions.q: Leonardo da Vinci's use of soft, smoky transitions between tones, avoiding harsh outlines, is called:
questions.explain: Sfumato is the subtle blending of tones and colours so that edges dissolve, as seen in the 'Mona Lisa'.
